zoom.note: Most often a verb: "zoom in" (make a picture bigger) or "zoom" (move very fast).

ex: My son loves scouting because he goes camping with friends.
Scouting teaches children useful skills like making a fire.
She has been active in scouting since she was eight.
Is there a scouting group for kids in our town?
The abuser was arrested after the neighbors called the police.
It took her years to finally leave her abuser.
This program helps people who live with an abuser.
An abuser often tries to control who you can see.
abuser.note: Also a person who uses drugs or alcohol too much: "a drug abuser".

ex: In the past, many homosexuals had to hide their private lives.
The old law sent homosexuals to prison.
The study compared homosexuals and heterosexuals of the same age.
Some countries still treat homosexuals as criminals.
homosexual.note: Mostly an adjective. As a noun it can sound offensive; say "a gay man" or "a gay person".

mage.note: Used mainly in fantasy; "wizard" is more common.

ex: The festival lineup was announced on the website today.
This year's lineup includes many young local bands.
Who is the main act in the lineup on Saturday?
The concert lineup looks great, so let's buy tickets now.
lineup.note: Often the players chosen for a game ("the starting lineup") or a set of products.

cheddar.note: Uncountable: some cheddar, a slice of cheddar. Often "cheddar cheese".

ex: The family lived on a small homestead far from town.
The old homestead still stands at the end of the road.
They built their homestead by hand from wood and stone.
Settlers got free land to start a homestead in the West.

coping.note: Mostly used in "coping skills/strategies" or "coping with".

ex: The young sportsman trains every day for the big race.
He was a great sportsman and won many medals.
A good sportsman shakes hands after losing a game.
My grandfather was a sportsman who played soccer and tennis.
sportsman.note: Often a man who hunts or fishes. For people who play sports, "athlete" is more common.

bust.note: Most often informal: "bust" = break or arrest; "go bust" = lose all your money.

ex: I'd like a large cappuccino and a croissant, please.
She drinks a cappuccino at the cafe every morning.
This little cafe near the station makes great cappuccinos.
Can I get a cappuccino with oat milk to go?
Carbon has several isotopes with different numbers of neutrons.
Doctors use this isotope to take pictures inside the body.
A radioactive isotope slowly breaks down over time.
Scientists measured the isotopes in the rock to find its age.

plateau.note: Also a time with no growth or change: "Sales reached a plateau."

blackjack.note: Uncountable: play blackjack, a game of blackjack (not "a blackjack").

ex: We bought a keg of beer for the party.
The keg is already empty, so we need another one.
Can you help me carry the keg to the car?
The bar puts in a new beer keg every night.

combo.note: Most often any mix of things: "a great combo"; also a meal set: "a burger combo".

ex: We played darts at the bar after work.
Darts is a popular game in British pubs.
He is very good at darts and often wins.
Do you want to play a game of darts?
darts.note: Takes a singular verb: "Darts is fun."

detergent.note: Usually uncountable: some detergent, laundry detergent, dish detergent.

minion.note: Usually negative or joking: a servant of a powerful person.

dong.note: Plural: "dong". Also the sound of a big bell; in slang it is a rude word.

ex: She joined the cheerleading team at her high school.
Cheerleading needs a lot of strength and skill.
The cheerleading competition is on Saturday afternoon.
He hurt his arm at cheerleading practice yesterday.

Protestant.note: Most often an adjective: "a Protestant church". Always written with a capital P.

ex: The intern helped the doctor during the night shift.
She is a medical intern at a big city hospital.
Every intern in this hospital works very long hours.
Ask the intern to check the patient's blood pressure.
intern.note: Most often a student who works for a short time to learn a job: "a summer intern".

ex: The two countries signed a memorandum on trade.
The government and the union signed a memorandum of understanding.
The memorandum explains how the two companies will work together.
The lawyers read the memorandum carefully before the meeting.
memorandum.note: Plural: "memoranda" or "memorandums"; an office note is usually a "memo".

ex: In Australia, a possum often lives in a tree near houses.
A possum ran across our roof in Sydney last night.
The possum sleeps during the day and eats at night.
We saw a cute possum with big eyes in the park.
possum.note: In the US "possum" usually means an opossum, a different animal from the Australian possum.

ex: Our terrier barks at every car that drives past.
The little terrier chased a rat across the yard.
Terriers are small dogs with a lot of energy.
She has two terriers and a cat at home.

team building.note: Uncountable: "We do team building," not "a team building."

bubble gum.note: Uncountable: "a piece of bubble gum", not "a bubble gum".

jet lag.note: Uncountable: "I have jet lag", not "a jet lag".

ginger ale.note: Uncountable: a glass of ginger ale, a can of ginger ale.
